title: Randomized sharer profiles for trust and closeness
why: Fixes the design cause: randomizing trust and tie removes confounding with real contact traits, and an opt-out answers U1.

power_target.basis: Observed close-tie 0.030 and trust-high 0.057; H2 MDE 0.0258 at n 6709/5256, so about 1,500 per cell clustered detects 0.03.

rationale: In the source study, close ties (+3.0 points) and high trust (+5.7 points; low-trust cell n=817) were measured on real contacts and bundle correlated traits. Randomly assigning vignette sharers' closeness and trustworthiness tests whether these associations survive randomization. A 'would not share' option removes the forced-choice link.
contribution: Provides randomized estimates of sharer closeness and trustworthiness effects on sharing across true, false and fact-check content.
hypothesis: Randomly assigned close and high-trust sharers raise sharing likelihood relative to distant and low-trust sharers (about 3 points), with effects possibly differing by information type.
primary_outcome: Sharing likelihood (0-100), with 'would not share' analysed separately as a binary outcome.
comparison: Close vs distant; high vs low trust; main effects pooled over information type, with exploratory interactions with information type.
unresolved: Actual post images and the headline pool must be supplied by the research team.
Compensation, IRB number and panel vendor are to be set by the research team.
label: Design advance

title: Fact-check effect by topic
why: Fixes the sample cause: randomizing topic with adequate health items answers U3.

power_target.basis: E2 health fact-check -0.028 (SE 0.028) versus political -0.151; difference of about 0.12 is detectable, but 0.04 targets a smaller health effect; MDE 0.031 at n~4,000 per arm.

rationale: In the source study fact-checks were shared 13.3 points less overall, but E2 shows the health estimate near zero (-0.028, SE 0.028) against about -0.15 for political items, with only about 1,100 health profiles and topic not randomized. Randomizing topic with a balanced item bank tests whether the penalty really differs by topic, and survey language is added because of language differences.
contribution: Provides a randomized, adequately powered test of whether the fact-check sharing penalty holds for health as for political claims, in English and Spanish.
hypothesis: The fact-check sharing penalty relative to true/neutral posts is smaller for health than for political items. Misinformation is shared less than true content in both topics. Exploratory: the topic difference varies by survey language.
primary_outcome: Share choice for each post (share vs. do not share), with an opt-out.
comparison: Fact-check versus true/neutral sharing, compared between health and political topic arms; information type varies within respondent.
unresolved: The item bank (at least 20 health and 20 political items in true, false and fact-check versions) and Spanish translations must be supplied by the research team.
Per-post randomization of information type is implemented in the survey platform; the embedded stimulus slots show one draw.
Panel vendor, compensation and IRB approval number need to be supplied.
label: Generalizability

title: Absolute versus relative misinformation sharing by belief
why: Fixes the measurement cause: single-item rating with an opt-out breaks the forced-choice link and answers U2.

power_target.basis: S3 differences of 0.055 to 0.056 with SE 0.017; the interaction across formats needs about double the cell size.

rationale: In the source study, respondents who believe more disputed claims shifted toward misinformation (+5.6 points) and away from true items (-5.5 points), a mirrored pattern that forced choice makes mechanically linked. Belief in disputed claims had no distinguishable overall effect on sharing (intervals about ±1.7 to 2.2 points). Independent single-headline sharing with a 'share nothing' option tests whether the belief slope for misinformation is absolute.
contribution: Separates absolute from relative belief-related misinformation sharing by breaking the forced-choice link between misinformation and true items.
hypothesis: In forced choice, belief in disputed claims predicts more misinformation and less true-content choice (mirrored). In single-item format, if the belief slope for misinformation sharing remains positive, the effect is absolute; if it is near zero while the true-content slope is negative or null, it is purely relative.
primary_outcome: Share of misinformation headlines shared (single format) or chosen (forced choice), by belief index.
comparison: Belief by information-type slope compared across formats (three-way interaction: format x belief x information type).
unresolved: Actual headline images and the final disputed-claim items must be supplied by the research team.
IRB approval number and compensation must be supplied by the research team.
label: Theoretical debate
